summary: Defines two new IKEv2 configuration attributes that carry the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses of the P-CSCF, a server in 3GPP's IP Multimedia Subsystem. An IPsec gateway can use them to tell a client where that server is.

plainLanguage.summary: When you join a network, it hands you the address of the helper you need to call. This adds a slot for that address.

questions: what is the p-cscf attribute in ikev2
how does an ipsec client find the p-cscf
subtitle: Adding a way for IPsec gateways to tell mobile clients where to find the IMS signaling server.

tldr.problem: Mobile devices accessing 3GPP networks through untrusted networks (like WiFi) need to know the address of the Proxy-Call Session Control Function (P-CSCF) that handles their IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) calls, but IKEv2 has no standard way to deliver this address.
tldr.mechanism: Two new IKEv2 configuration attributes are defined: one carries an IPv4 address of the P-CSCF, and one carries an IPv6 address. An IPsec gateway (ePDG) can include these in its IKEv2 response when a client connects.
tldr.outcome: Mobile clients can request and receive P-CSCF addresses from the IPsec gateway, eliminating the need for static configuration and allowing them to access IMS services securely.

today: RFC 7651 is an Informational RFC that adds two new IKEv2 configuration attributes. It has not been obsoleted and is part of the 3GPP system architecture for allowing mobile devices to access IMS services through untrusted networks.

sections.title: The Problem: Finding IMS on Untrusted Networks
sections.content:
The 3GPP architecture defines a way for mobile devices to connect to cellular networks through untrusted access points (like public WiFi). The mobile device sets up an IPsec tunnel to an Evolved Packet Data Gateway (ePDG), a security gateway. The ePDG then tunnels the traffic into the home network using either Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) or GTP.

But if the device wants to use IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) services (calls, messages), it needs to know the address of a Proxy-Call Session Control Function (P-CSCF) server in the home network. IMS is built on SIP, and the P-CSCF acts as the SIP outbound proxy for the mobile device. Currently, there was no way for the ePDG to tell the client this address through IKEv2, so devices had to be statically configured with it.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile devices connect to home networks through WiFi gateways. To make calls via that home network, they need the address of a special call-routing server. IKEv2 had no way to deliver that address, so phones had to be configured with it beforehand.

sections.title: The Solution Overview
sections.content:
The 3GPP architecture used the IPsec gateway (ePDG) to set up encrypted tunnels and deliver configuration parameters. Instead of forcing clients to be statically configured with P-CSCF addresses, this specification leverages IKEv2's existing configuration mechanism to deliver them dynamically.

The solution is elegant and minimal: two new configuration attributes are defined that fit seamlessly into IKEv2's standard configuration payload exchange. No new protocol messages or handshakes are needed, just two new attribute types that the gateway can include in its response when a client requests them.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of hardcoding the P-CSCF address into the phone, the gateway can tell the phone where it is when they connect. It uses the same mechanism IKEv2 already uses to deliver other configuration.

sections.title: The Two New Attributes
sections.content:
The specification adds two new IKEv2 configuration attributes. The P_CSCF_IP4_ADDRESS attribute (type 20) carries a 4-octet IPv4 address. The P_CSCF_IP6_ADDRESS attribute (type 21) carries a 16-octet IPv6 address. Both follow the standard IKEv2 configuration attribute format with a type field, length field, and address field.

When a length of zero is used, the attribute acts as a request indicator: the mobile client includes it to ask the ePDG for P-CSCF addresses. The ePDG may respond with zero, one, or more attributes of each type. If multiple addresses are provided in one message, they are unordered unless a system architecture imposes an order.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new fields are added to IKEv2 messages: one for IPv4 P-CSCF addresses and one for IPv6 addresses. The client can ask for them, and the gateway can send back one or more.

sections.title: Example Exchange
sections.content:
In a typical exchange, the mobile client sends an IKEv2 AUTH message with a configuration payload (CFG_REQUEST) asking for several things: INTERNAL_IP4_ADDRESS (an IP address to use), INTERNAL_IP4_DNS (a DNS server), and P_CSCF_IP4_ADDRESS (the P-CSCF address). The ePDG responds with a configuration payload (CFG_REPLY) containing the assigned IP address, the P-CSCF address (possibly multiple addresses), and the DNS server.

The P-CSCF addresses are included among other configuration parameters in the standard IKEv2 configuration exchange. Once the client has the P-CSCF address, it can perform SIP registration and initiate IMS calls through the P-CSCF.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone asks for its IP address, DNS, and the P-CSCF address all in one message. The gateway sends them all back together.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
This specification extends IKEv2 and inherits all of IKEv2's security properties. The new P-CSCF address attributes are exchanged as part of the standard IKEv2 configuration payload, which is already protected by IKEv2's integrity and privacy mechanisms. The specification does not introduce new security vulnerabilities: the ePDG is trusted by the mobile device (they have already authenticated each other through IKEv2), so delivering configuration through IKEv2 is safe.

The benefits of dynamic delivery outweigh static configuration: clients no longer need to be pre-provisioned with P-CSCF addresses, reducing operational complexity and eliminating configuration errors.
sections.plainLanguage: IKEv2 already protects everything, so adding two new address fields does not create any new security problems. The gateway is trusted, so the addresses it sends are trustworthy.
